summaries.example: Imagine you write a note saying, “If I become very sick and cannot understand things anymore, do not give me a certain treatment.” Years later, you have severe memory problems but still enjoy music and being with family. Should people follow your old note? Philosophers ask whether the later person is still you, and whether your earlier wishes should still guide care.
summaries.summary: Personal identity means being one individual who continues through time. This topic matters because we make plans for our future, remember past actions, and make choices about care and responsibility. One philosophical view says that mental connections—such as memories, goals, beliefs, and personality—are most important. Another says that the continuing human organism is most important. A strange imagined case, such as one mind continuing in two people, suggests that being the very same individual may not be the only thing that matters. Perhaps what matters is how strongly a later person is connected to an earlier person. These ideas affect questions about future pain, blame and punishment, early human life, death, medical instructions, and fairness between people. The entry explains that there is no settled answer: identity and the things that matter ethically might come apart.
key_ideas: Philosophers disagree about what makes someone the same person over time.
Some focus on memories, plans, and personality. Others focus on the continuing living body.
What makes us the same person may not be exactly what matters for caring, blame, promises, or medical choices.
Questions about beginnings and endings of life can depend on whether mental links or bodily life matter more.
People are separate individuals, so one person’s good and another person’s good are not automatically the same thing.
summaries.why_it_matters: This topic helps us think carefully about promises, punishment, medical care, and how much to care about our future selves. It also reminds us that difficult moral questions may depend on more than one kind of connection. Philosophers can agree that a question is important while still disagreeing about the best answer.

important_terms.definition: Being the very same individual at different times, such as being the same child and adult.
The mental links between a person at different times, such as memories, plans, beliefs, and feelings.
The idea that a person remains the same because the same living human body continues.
A special kind of care for your own future, such as saving money for yourself later.

questions_to_think_about: If someone changes greatly, what might still make them the same person?
Should a person’s old medical wishes be followed after severe memory loss?
Is caring about your future different from caring about a friend’s future?
Can a person be responsible for something they did long ago if they no longer remember it?

summaries.example: Suppose a person signs an advance directive refusing life-extending treatment if they later develop severe dementia. When that time comes, the person seems content and enjoys ordinary activities but can no longer make complex judgments about life as a whole. One approach says the directive should be honored because biological continuity preserves the person’s identity. Another asks whether the directive’s force depends on psychological continuity, earlier values, or the later person’s remaining capacity to value. The case shows why identity and what ethically matters may be different questions.
summaries.summary: The entry examines how theories of personal identity shape ethical judgments. Here, identity concerns numerical sameness across time, not social identity such as gender, ethnicity, nationality, or sexual orientation. The main metaphysical alternatives are psychological and biological. A psychological criterion identifies a person through uniquely continuing mental relations. Continuity is a chain of overlapping connections; connectedness refers to particular links, such as a memory or intention, which can vary in strength. A biological criterion instead emphasizes the persistence of the human organism. The fission case suggests that psychological continuity can survive without one-to-one numerical identity, leading some philosophers to say that identity itself is not what matters. These distinctions affect prudential concern, responsibility, medical directives, and questions at the beginning and end of life. They also influence normative ethics: the separateness of persons can be invoked against unrestricted aggregation, but it has been used to support competing theories, including egalitarianism, libertarianism, contractualism, and forms of egoism. The entry ends with a methodological question: do ethical principles depend on an independently correct account of identity, or do ethical ideals help determine which relations matter?
key_ideas: Psychological theories distinguish numerical identity from psychological continuity and connectedness. A person may have an overlapping mental life even when direct connections become weak.

The branching or fission case challenges the idea that numerical identity alone explains what matters: one earlier psychology might continue in two later people, although one thing cannot be numerically identical with two things.
Biological theories identify a person with a continuing human organism. Their defenders can still say that psychological relations are what matter for responsibility or self-concern.
Identity does not automatically settle practical questions. A person may remain biologically identical while losing the psychological relations that support special concern or accountability.
The debate appears in questions about abortion, death, dementia, advance directives, responsibility, and the distribution of benefits and burdens.
Appeals to the separateness of persons have been used to support egalitarian, libertarian, contractualist, anti-aggregation, and other views. Separateness alone may not determine one ethical theory.
summaries.why_it_matters: Our views about persistence through time influence how we understand future interests, accountability, punishment, medical decisions, and justice. The discussion also warns against assuming that one answer to “Who is the same person?” automatically answers “What should we care about?” Keeping those questions distinct makes room for more careful reasoning about cases involving memory loss, radical change, early life, death, and conflicts between individual claims.

important_terms.definition: Numerical sameness: one individual’s persistence through time, unlike qualitative similarity between two different individuals.
An overlapping chain of psychological connections, including memories, intentions, beliefs, desires, and character traits.
Particular direct mental links between stages of a life; these links can exist by degrees and may weaken over time.
The view that identity consists in the continuing life of a human organism, whether or not psychological abilities are present.
Special concern for one’s own future welfare, often called egoistic or prudential concern.
Being an appropriate target of praise, blame, punishment, or compensation for an action.
The fact that different people are distinct individuals with separate lives, claims, and experiences.
An approach giving extra moral weight to benefits for people who are worse off, without simply maximizing total benefit.

questions_to_think_about: If psychological continuity branches into two people, should concern for each successor equal concern for one ordinary future self?
Can biological identity remain intact while the ethical reasons for blame or special concern substantially weaken?
Should an advance directive made by a competent person control treatment after severe dementia, and why?
Does the separateness of persons criticize utilitarian trade-offs, or can it support several different moral theories?
Should theories of personal identity be fixed before ethical theory, or should each help shape the other?

summaries.example: Imagine that a science-fiction machine divides one person’s mental patterns between two healthy people. Both new people remember the person’s life, share the person’s plans, and have a similar personality. They cannot both be literally the one original person, because one individual cannot be two separate individuals. Still, it seems reasonable for the original person to care about both of them. This suggests that mental connection might matter even when exact identity does not.
summaries.summary: Personal identity is the question of what makes an individual persist from one time to another. The entry separates this question from social identity, which can involve affiliations, gender, race, sexuality, values, and experiences. Two major answers are considered. The psychological view emphasizes an appropriately connected mental life: memories, intentions, beliefs, desires, and character can form an overlapping chain across time. The biological view emphasizes continuity of the living human organism, even when psychological abilities are missing. A branching case creates a problem for identity-based theories because one earlier person could have two psychologically continuous successors, although numerical identity cannot divide in that way. Some philosophers therefore argue that psychological continuity or connectedness is what matters for future concern and perhaps morality. The distinction affects responsibility, punishment, advance directives, abortion arguments, definitions of death, and concern for people at different stages of life. The entry also connects personal identity with justice. Since each person has a separate life, some philosophers resist simply adding everyone’s benefits and harms together; others think weaker boundaries between stages of a life reduce the importance of separateness. Finally, the entry considers whether ethics should begin with a theory of identity or whether ethical ideals help shape our understanding of personal unity.
key_ideas: The entry focuses on identity as persistence through time, not on social or political identity.
Psychological theories emphasize continuing mental life. They may focus on identity itself, continuity, connectedness, or both.
The fission thought experiment separates identity from psychological continuity and motivates the view that relations between mental states may matter more than identity.
The biological theory says that a person is a continuing human organism, but it can allow psychological relations to matter for ethics.
Memory loss, personal change, and dementia raise different questions about future concern, responsibility, and medical decisions.
The separateness of persons matters in debates about fairness. Philosophers disagree about whether it supports equality, limits on adding benefits together, individual freedom, or other principles.
summaries.why_it_matters: People make commitments to future selves, judge others for past actions, and decide how resources and protections should be shared. Personal identity theories give different explanations of why these practices make sense. Studying the disagreement encourages students to distinguish factual questions about persistence from normative questions about what deserves concern, respect, blame, or protection.

important_terms.definition: Being one and the same individual across time, rather than merely resembling another individual.
Mental links that continue through time, including memories, plans, beliefs, desires, and parts of a person’s character.
A direct mental link between two times, such as remembering an event or keeping an intention; connectedness can be stronger or weaker.
The view that the same living human organism continues, even during times when ordinary mental abilities are absent.
A special reason to care about your own future well-being.
Being answerable for an action in a way that can make praise, blame, punishment, or compensation appropriate.
The idea that people are separate individuals, not one large person whose benefits and harms can simply be added together.
A view that gives greater moral importance to equal-sized benefits received by worse-off people.

questions_to_think_about: If a person changes their beliefs and personality over many years, should concern for their future become weaker?
Why might continuity matter more than direct memory for responsibility?
Could the same person remain biologically continuous while no longer having the mental abilities that support blame?
When helping one person conflicts with helping several others, should their claims be added together?
Should our moral ideas influence which kind of personal continuity we think matters?
